stem_md: In a vacuum calorimetry experiment, high-energy plasma discharges between $\ce{Ti(s)}$ electrodes are used to electrolyze water in dilute $\ce{KOH(aq)}$. During an experiment, the electrical input is 500. kJ and the calorimeter records 610. kJ of heat release into the surroundings. Which best explains this experimental result?

options.label: A
options.text_md: The electrodes undergo partial oxidation, an additional reaction not accounted for in electrolysis.

options.label: B
options.text_md: The system’s large specific heat capacity increases the total heat registered per unit of electrical energy.

options.label: C
options.text_md: The overall process is endothermic, so the surroundings must release heat to maintain equilibrium.

options.label: D
options.text_md: The entropy increase from gas formation causes the system to do work, resulting in additional temperature rise.

stem_md:
The standard enthalpy of combustion of ethyne can be estimated from the tabulated bond dissociation enthalpies (BDE) shown below to be –982 kJ mol$^{-1}$. The experimental $\Delta H^\circ_\text{combustion}$ is –1256 kJ mol$^{-1}$. Which is the best explanation for the discrepancy?

Bond BDE (kJ mol$^{-1}$)

$\ce{C#C}$ 839

$\ce{C-H}$ 412

$\ce{O=O}$ 498

$\ce{C=O}$ 741

$\ce{O-H}$ 463

$\ce{C2H2(g) + 2.5 O2(g) -> 2 CO2(g) + H2O(g)}$ $\Delta H^\circ_\text{expt}$ = –1256 kJ mol$^{-1}$

options.label: A
options.text_md: The tabulated $\ce{C-H}$ BDE does not account for the unusual strength of the bond formed to the sp- hybridized carbon in $\ce{C2H2}$.

options.label: B
options.text_md: The tabulated $\ce{O=O}$ BDE does not account for the unusual weakness of the bond in dioxygen due to its paramagnetism.

options.label: C
options.text_md: The tabulated $\ce{C=O}$ BDE does not account for the stabilization due to electronic delocalization in carbon dioxide.

options.label: D
options.text_md: The tabulated $\ce{O-H}$ BDE does not account for the stabilization due to hydrogen bonding in water.

source: USNCO 2026 Local exam, question 23. © American Chemical Society; reproduced for non-commercial practice.
